title: Half is enough (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:13)
hook: no one leaves the world with even half their desires fulfilled
tomorrow: Abraham and Moses pleaded and weren't answered. who was?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a baby's closed fists and an old man's open hands: we arrive grabbing and leave letting go. Hands open at the end. Today, a sage does the math on all the grabbing in between.
screen: `HANDS OPEN AT THE END.` → `THE GRABBING IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: One in the morning. The cart has five things in it, and the plan was one. The app offers a sixth, a slightly better version of the third. A bar at the top says free shipping is only a few dollars away. The thumb hovers, then taps. The screen says thank you. And before the box has even left the warehouse, a new tab is open, looking at the next thing. Nobody in this scene is a villain. This is just what wanting does. A midrash on Ecclesiastes saw this exact loop, long before anyone had a cart.
screen: `ONE IN THE MORNING. FIVE THINGS.` → `THE PLAN WAS ONE.` → `A NEW TAB, ALREADY.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes says it plainly: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver." The midrash, Ecclesiastes Rabbah, turns that line into arithmetic. No one, it says, leaves the world with even half of what they wanted in hand. Have a hundred, and you want two hundred. Reach two hundred, and you want four hundred. Watch what the math does. Every gain doubles the finish line, so the half you were chasing slides further off each time. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: by the midrash's math, the more you get, the further you are from half. So the sages don't promise that one day you'll finally have it all. They point the other way. If half can't be reached by adding, then enough has to come from somewhere else: from choosing. Elsewhere, in Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma asks, who is rich? His answer: the one who is happy with their portion. Not the one with the most. The one who stepped out of the doubling. This isn't a vow to own nothing. Jewish blessings are said over bread, over wine, over new clothes. It's one small exit from the loop: name a want, and let it go unfed. Half is enough, because the whole was never coming.
screen: `MORE SILVER, NOT SATISFIED.` · `HAVE 100, WANT 200.` · `THE FINISH LINE DOUBLES.` · `ENOUGH COMES FROM CHOOSING.` · then, large: `HALF IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Open the place your wants collect: a cart, a wishlist, a row of tabs, a note of things to buy. Choose one item and remove it, just for today, and look at what's left once that one stops doubling. If nothing is saved anywhere, name one want quietly to yourself and let it sit there, unfed, while the sit runs.
screen: `THE CART, THE LIST, THE TABS.` · `REMOVE ONE.` · `LET IT SIT, UNFED.`

segments.voice: Half is enough: the midrash's arithmetic of wanting. Have a hundred, want two hundred; nobody reaches half by adding.
Your line: half is enough. The whole was never coming anyway. Thirty days into reading midrash.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on contentment often turns to Ben Zoma in Pirkei Avot 4:1: who is rich? the one who rejoices in their portion. Blessings over food and new things are one daily way the tradition practices enough.

fork.setup: your cousin just got a raise and is already pricing a bigger apartment, a newer car and a second phone. by the midrash, what's the honest question to ask her?
options: how much would be enough, since the finish line keeps doubling?
can you afford it, since debt is the only real danger here?
why want anything at all, since wanting is the real problem?
fork.reveal: Ecclesiastes Rabbah doesn't condemn wanting; it shows the finish line doubling with every gain. enough has to be chosen.

chat.says: saba's selling the house. one-bedroom apartment. mom says he keeps a third. i want to save EVERYTHING.
options: Save what you love, not all of it. Wanting all of it is the doubling.
Rent a storage unit for it all. Then nobody has to let go of anything.
Save nothing. The midrash says wanting things is the problem, so skip it.
chat.meaning: The midrash says no one reaches half by adding more. Enough is chosen, not reached, and it isn't a call to own nothing.
